title: The Skeleton That Listens
paragraphs: A dry bone on a museum shelf looks like stone, and the look is wrong.
In a living body the skeleton is tissue: supplied with blood, served by nerves, and taken apart and rebuilt without pause.
By a common estimate roughly a tenth of the adult skeleton is replaced each year.
The material is collagen, the protein of tendon, stiffened by crystals of a calcium phosphate mineral called hydroxyapatite that make up roughly two thirds of its weight.
The mineral supplies hardness, the collagen keeps the bone from shattering, and the whole structure doubles as a reserve holding about 99 percent of the body's calcium.
Three kinds of cell do the work.
Osteoblasts build, laying down a soft collagen matrix called osteoid that hardens as mineral forms inside it.

Osteoclasts demolish: large cells with many nuclei, drawn from the same blood-forming lineage as macrophages, they seal themselves against a bone surface, pump acid into the sealed space to dissolve the mineral, and release enzymes to digest the collagen.

The third cell is the least famous and the most numerous: when osteoblasts finish building, some are walled in by their own product and become osteocytes, each living in a small chamber called a lacuna and reaching its neighbors through hair-thin channels called canaliculi.
Osteocytes make up more than 90 percent of the cells in bone and form a network threading the entire skeleton.
Building and demolishing follow a sequence that the American orthopedic surgeon Harold Frost named the basic multicellular unit in the 1960s: a team of cells moving through bone like a road crew.
Osteoclasts arrive first and carve a cavity, a job that takes roughly three weeks.
After a brief pause, osteoblasts fill the cavity with new osteoid over about three months, and the fresh matrix then spends further months hardening.
A full cycle at one site runs four to six months, and in a healthy young adult the amounts removed and replaced closely match, a balance physiologists call coupling.

Trabecular bone, the lattice inside the vertebrae and the ends of long bones, holds about a fifth of the skeleton's mass but turns over several times faster than the dense cortical bone of the shafts.
Why rebuild a structure that already works?
Remodeling repairs the microscopic cracks of daily loading, releases calcium when the blood runs short, and lets the skeleton adjust its mass to the loads it carries.

The balance does not hold forever: bone mass peaks around age 30 and then declines slowly, because each cycle replaces slightly less than it removes, and in women the loss speeds up after menopause, when falling estrogen frees osteoclasts.
Over decades the deficits add up, and the porous, brittle bone of osteoporosis results.

That bone answers to load was noticed before anyone could explain it: in 1867 the anatomist Georg Hermann von Meyer published drawings of the lattice inside the upper end of the thigh bone, and Karl Culmann, an engineer in Zurich, remarked that the lattice followed the same curves as the stress lines he had drawn for a crane.
The German surgeon Julius Wolff took up the idea and in 1892 published a book arguing that bone reshapes itself by mathematical rules until its architecture matches the forces it bears.
The claim has been known ever since as Wolff's law, and I think the title flatters it.
Later critics faulted his mathematics, and his tidy right-angle lattices are not quite what one finds in a real femur.
What survives is the plainer observation underneath: bone is laid down where it is stressed and removed where it is not, and that observation has held up remarkably well.

Frost gave that observation its modern form in the 1980s with the mechanostat, named by analogy with a thermostat: the osteocyte network measures strain, the slight stretching and squeezing of bone under load, against two set points.
Strain below the lower set point marks bone as surplus to be removed, strain above the upper one calls for more bone, and between the two the tissue is maintained.
The model predicts that bone responds locally rather than throughout the body, and the evidence agrees.
A 1977 study of professional tennis players found the cortex of the upper arm bone in the playing arm roughly a third thicker than in the other arm.
Swimmers and cyclists, whose sports spare the skeleton, tend to have lighter bones than runners and weight lifters.
How does a cell buried in rock feel a load?
The leading explanation is that bending a bone squeezes fluid through the canaliculi past the osteocytes' processes, and the drag of that flow is what the cells detect.
They answer with chemistry: osteocytes secrete a protein called sclerostin that acts as a brake on osteoblasts; loading turns the secretion down and unloading turns it up.

People born without working sclerostin, a rare condition called sclerosteosis, grow bone so dense that the skull can pinch the nerves passing through it; an antibody against sclerostin is now an approved osteoporosis drug.

Osteocytes also govern demolition, releasing a signal called RANKL that osteoclast precursors must receive before they can mature into working osteoclasts, and releasing more of it when neighbors die, as happens in damaged or unloaded bone.
The sharpest demonstration is removing load altogether.
In orbit, where nothing presses on the skeleton, astronauts on the International Space Station have lost bone mineral from the hip and lower spine at roughly 1 to 1.5 percent a month.
The bones of the forearm and skull, which carry no body weight even on Earth, are largely spared.
The calcium freed by the extra demolition leaves in the urine, raising the risk of kidney stones.
Recovery after landing is slower than the loss, and a year back on the ground is often not enough to restore what six months in orbit removed.
There is evidence, too, that the trabecular lattice, once lost, is not fully rebuilt even when overall density looks normal again.
One need not leave the planet to see the same effect.

Space agencies mimic it by paying healthy volunteers to lie for weeks or months with the head tilted six degrees below the feet, which shifts fluid toward the head as weightlessness does and takes all weight off the legs.

Their bones thin at rates close to those seen in orbit, and the bedridden patient and the person paralyzed below the waist show the same pattern, losing bone from exactly the limbs that have stopped bearing weight.
The skeleton, in other words, runs a strict economy.
Tissue that is not loaded is treated as surplus and spent, and the osteocytes, not gravity or the vacuum of space, are the accountants.
If unloading drains bone, loading should refill it, but what kind?

Experiments in the 1980s on turkey wing bones showed that a steady, unchanging load did nothing to prevent bone loss, while a load applied and released a few dozen times a day was enough to maintain the bone and sometimes to add to it.
What bone seems to want is loading that is dynamic rather than static, forceful rather than prolonged, and unusual in its direction.

That rule explains a finding I find sobering: walking, the exercise most often recommended to older adults, does less for the hip and spine than most assume, because it loads the skeleton in exactly the way it is used to.

Since late 2008 the space station has carried a resistance machine built around vacuum cylinders, and crews who train hard on it lose markedly less bone by standard density scans, though finer measures of bone structure still record a loss.
The picture that emerges is of a tissue in permanent negotiation with its own use.
Osteoblasts and osteoclasts are the parties at the table, but the osteocytes, listening for the push of fluid, set the terms.
I would not go as far as the enthusiasts who promise that the right exercise can rebuild any bone at any age; an old skeleton answers more faintly than a young one.
But the lesson of the astronauts and the bed rest volunteers runs both ways, and a skeleton that is asked, often and forcefully, to do its job will generally do it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the hydroxyapatite in bone
choices: is a form of collagen that keeps bone from shattering under load
makes up about 99 percent of the tissue's weight
is a calcium phosphate mineral that gives bone its hardness
is replaced in its entirety roughly once every ten years
is produced by osteoclasts as they dissolve older bone surfaces

proof.quote: a calcium phosphate mineral called hydroxyapatite
The mineral supplies hardness

questions.why: Paragraph 1 names hydroxyapatite as a calcium phosphate mineral and then says the mineral supplies hardness while the collagen keeps the bone from shattering.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 1 says collagen, not the mineral, keeps bone from shattering.
Wrong number: 99 percent is the share of the body's calcium that bone holds; the mineral is about two thirds of the tissue's weight.
Wrong detail: a tenth of the skeleton is replaced each year, and nothing says the mineral is replaced in its entirety.
Reversed: paragraph 2 says osteoclasts dissolve mineral; osteoblasts lay down the matrix that mineralizes.

questions.stem: According to the passage, osteoclasts break down bone by
choices: pumping acid into a sealed space and releasing enzymes that digest collagen
walling themselves into chambers from which they dissolve the surrounding mineral
laying down a soft matrix that draws calcium out of the hardened bone around it
cutting hair-thin channels through the mineral so that fluid can wash it away
secreting a protein called sclerostin that dissolves the mineral crystals

proof.quote: pump acid into the sealed space to dissolve the mineral, and release enzymes to digest the collagen

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says osteoclasts seal themselves against a bone surface, pump acid into the sealed space to dissolve the mineral, and release enzymes to digest the collagen.
distractorNotes: Wrong cell: being walled into chambers is how osteoblasts become osteocytes, later in paragraph 2.
Reversed: laying down soft matrix is the osteoblasts' job, and that matrix hardens rather than dissolving anything.
Wrong detail: the hair-thin canaliculi are channels that connect osteocytes, not a demolition method.
Wrong paragraph: sclerostin in paragraph 7 is an osteocyte protein that brakes osteoblasts; it dissolves nothing.

questions.stem: All of the following are stated in the passage about osteocytes EXCEPT:
choices: They begin as osteoblasts that become walled in by their own product.
They make up more than 90 percent of the cells in bone.
They live in small chambers called lacunae.
They reach their neighbors through channels called canaliculi.
They are descended from the same lineage as macrophages.

proof.quote: walled in by their own product and become osteocytes
more than 90 percent of the cells in bone
a small chamber called a lacuna
reaching its neighbors through hair-thin channels called canaliculi
drawn from the same blood-forming lineage as macrophages

questions.why: Paragraph 2 gives the macrophage lineage to osteoclasts, not osteocytes. The other four statements all come from the last two sentences of paragraph 2.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 2, sentence 4 says some osteoblasts are walled in by their own product and become osteocytes.
Paragraph 2, sentence 5 says osteocytes make up more than 90 percent of the cells in bone.
Paragraph 2, sentence 4 says each lives in a small chamber called a lacuna.
Paragraph 2, sentence 4 says they reach their neighbors through hair-thin channels called canaliculi.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in a single remodeling cycle
choices: osteoblasts arrive first and prepare the surface that osteoclasts later clear
resorption takes about three weeks and formation about three months
osteoclasts and osteoblasts work on the same cavity at the same time
the whole sequence from start to finish lasts roughly three weeks
the new matrix hardens fully before the osteoblasts have finished filling the cavity

proof.quote: a job that takes roughly three weeks
over about three months

questions.why: Paragraph 3 gives the timeline: osteoclasts carve the cavity in roughly three weeks, then osteoblasts fill it over about three months, with further months of hardening after that.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 3 says osteoclasts arrive first.
Contradicted: osteoblasts follow after a brief pause, so the two phases are sequential.
Wrong number: three weeks is the resorption phase alone; the full cycle runs four to six months.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says the fresh matrix spends further months hardening after the cavity is filled.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Karl Culmann contributed to the idea behind Wolff's law by
choices: publishing detailed drawings of the lattice inside the upper end of the thigh bone
arguing in an 1892 book that bone follows mathematical rules
measuring the forces that act on a crane during lifting
noticing that the bone's lattice matched the stress lines of a crane
proving that trabeculae meet at right angles in a real femur

proof.quote: remarked that the lattice followed the same curves as the stress lines he had drawn for a crane

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says Culmann, an engineer in Zurich, remarked that von Meyer's lattice followed the same curves as the stress lines he had drawn for a crane.
distractorNotes: Wrong person: the drawings were published by von Meyer.
Wrong person: the 1892 book was Wolff's.
Outside the passage: Culmann drew stress lines for a crane on paper; nothing says he measured forces during lifting.
Reversed: paragraph 5 says Wolff's tidy right-angle lattices are not quite what one finds in a real femur.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Wolff's law is best described as
choices: respectful but qualified
openly contemptuous
enthusiastically uncritical
detached and neutral
puzzled and uncertain

proof.quote: I think the title flatters it
that observation has held up remarkably well

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says the title of law flatters the claim and that critics faulted Wolff's mathematics, yet it credits the plainer observation underneath as having held up remarkably well. That is respect with reservations.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the author faults the mathematics but keeps and praises the core observation.
Reversed: the author openly criticizes the law's title and its mathematics.
Too weak: the author takes a personal position with the words I think.
Wrong register: the author states clearly what fails and what survives.

questions.stem: The author mentions the study of tennis players in paragraph 6 primarily to
choices: show that diet and hormones have little effect on the adult skeleton
argue that racket sports are the best exercise for building bone
illustrate that bone responds to load locally rather than throughout the body
explain why swimmers and cyclists tend to have lighter bones than runners
demonstrate that the two set points of the mechanostat can be measured directly

proof.quote: The model predicts that bone responds locally rather than throughout the body, and the evidence agrees.

questions.why: Paragraph 6 sets up the study with a prediction, that bone responds locally rather than throughout the body, and the one-arm difference in the players is offered as the evidence that agrees.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: diet and hormones are never discussed in connection with the players.
Outside the passage: the author never ranks sports or recommends tennis.
Wrong detail: the swimmers and cyclists are a separate sentence making a related point, not what the tennis study explains.
Outside the passage: nothing says the set points were measured in the players.

questions.stem: According to the passage, mechanical loading of a bone causes osteocytes to
choices: release more sclerostin, which speeds the work of osteoblasts
raise the RANKL signal so that osteoclast precursors mature
die and summon a demolition crew to the site
secrete an antibody that neutralizes sclerostin in the matrix
secrete less sclerostin, easing a brake on osteoblasts

proof.quote: acts as a brake on osteoblasts; loading turns the secretion down and unloading turns it up

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says sclerostin is a brake on osteoblasts and that loading turns its secretion down while unloading turns it up.
distractorNotes: Reversed twice: loading lowers sclerostin, and sclerostin brakes osteoblasts rather than speeding them.
Reversed: paragraph 7 ties more RANKL to osteocytes dying in damaged or unloaded bone, not to loading.
Reversed: osteocytes die in bone that is damaged or starved of load.
Wrong source: the antibody against sclerostin is a drug, not something the cells secrete.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a drug blocking the RANKL signal would most likely
choices: prevent osteoblasts from being walled into the matrix as osteocytes
reduce the number of osteoclasts able to resorb bone
increase the amount of sclerostin released by osteocytes
raise urinary calcium by freeing mineral from the skeleton
shorten the time osteoblasts need to fill a cavity

proof.quote: a signal called RANKL that osteoclast precursors must receive before they can mature into working osteoclasts

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says osteoclast precursors must receive RANKL before they can mature into working osteoclasts. Block the signal and fewer precursors mature, so less bone is resorbed.
distractorNotes: Unrelated: the walling-in of osteoblasts in paragraph 2 has nothing to do with RANKL.
Unrelated: the passage ties sclerostin to loading, not to RANKL.
Reversed: fewer osteoclasts would mean less mineral freed, not more; the urinary calcium rise in paragraph 8 comes from extra demolition.
Unrelated: the passage ties RANKL to osteoclasts, and nothing connects it to how fast osteoblasts work.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if the fluid in the canaliculi could not move, a loaded bone would most likely
choices: be sensed as overloaded and gain mass above the upper set point
shift its remodeling from the cortical bone to the trabecular lattice
respond with a stronger RANKL signal from the osteoclasts themselves
behave as if it were unloaded, with sclerostin secretion rising
harden faster, since the osteoid would no longer be disturbed

proof.quote: the drag of that flow is what the cells detect
loading turns the secretion down and unloading turns it up

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says the drag of fluid flow is what osteocytes detect, and that unloading turns sclerostin up. If the fluid cannot move, the cells would detect no load, and the chemistry would follow the unloaded path.
distractorNotes: Reversed: without the flow the cells would detect less load, not more.
Unrelated: the cortical and trabecular contrast in paragraph 3 is about turnover rate, not sensing.
Wrong cell: RANKL in paragraph 7 comes from osteocytes, not osteoclasts.
Outside the passage: nothing links osteoid hardening to the movement of canalicular fluid.

questions.stem: According to the passage, all of the following are true of bone loss during long spaceflights EXCEPT:
choices: It affects the skull and forearm about as much as the hip.
It proceeds at roughly 1 to 1.5 percent a month in the hip and lower spine.
It raises the risk of kidney stones.
It is not fully reversed within a year of landing in many cases.
It may leave the trabecular lattice incompletely rebuilt even after density recovers.

proof.quote: 1 to 1.5 percent a month
raising the risk of kidney stones
a year back on the ground is often not enough
not fully rebuilt even when overall density looks normal again
The bones of the forearm and skull, which carry no body weight even on Earth, are largely spared.

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the forearm and skull, which carry no body weight even on Earth, are largely spared. The other four statements are all in paragraph 8.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 8, sentence 2 gives the rate of 1 to 1.5 percent a month for the hip and lower spine.
Paragraph 8, sentence 4 says the freed calcium raises the risk of kidney stones.
Paragraph 8, sentence 5 says a year back on the ground is often not enough.
Paragraph 8, sentence 6 says the trabecular lattice is not fully rebuilt even when density looks normal.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the earliest measurable bone loss in a newly arrived astronaut would most likely appear in
choices: the shafts of the long bones, where dense cortical bone makes up most of the mass
the skull, where the fluid shift of weightlessness is greatest
the forearm, which carries no body weight even on Earth
the collagen fibers rather than the mineral crystals
the vertebrae, where fast-turning trabecular bone is concentrated

proof.quote: the lattice inside the vertebrae and the ends of long bones
turns over several times faster than the dense cortical bone of the shafts
lost bone mineral from the hip and lower spine

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says trabecular bone, the lattice inside the vertebrae and the ends of long bones, turns over several times faster than cortical bone, and paragraph 8 reports the losses from the hip and lower spine. The fastest-cycling sites are where a shift in the balance would show first.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 3 says the cortical bone of the shafts turns over several times more slowly.
Contradicted: paragraph 8 says the skull is largely spared.
Contradicted: paragraph 8 says the forearm is largely spared because it carries no body weight.
Outside the passage: the losses are reported as bone mineral, and nothing suggests collagen goes first.

questions.stem: The author describes bed rest studies in paragraph 9 primarily to
choices: warn that prolonged hospital stays cause even more bone loss than long spaceflights
show that the loss in orbit comes from unloading rather than from space itself
explain how space agencies select the volunteers for their missions
introduce the vacuum-cylinder machine that astronauts use to exercise
argue that fluid shifting toward the head is the main cause of bone loss

proof.quote: One need not leave the planet to see the same effect.
the osteocytes, not gravity or the vacuum of space, are the accountants

questions.why: Paragraph 9 opens by saying one need not leave the planet to see the same effect and closes by crediting the osteocytes, not gravity or the vacuum of space. The bed rest studies isolate unloading as the cause.
distractorNotes: Wrong comparison: paragraph 9 says the rates are close to those in orbit, not greater.
Outside the passage: the volunteers are paid to lie in bed, and nothing about mission selection is said.
Wrong paragraph: the resistance machine appears in paragraph 10.
Wrong emphasis: the fluid shift is mentioned as a way the posture mimics weightlessness; the paragraph blames the absence of load.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 9, the word 'economy' most nearly means
choices: the system of trade and production in a nation
a period of financial hardship or scarcity
a careful and thrifty management of resources
the cheapest class of service available
a branch of knowledge about money and markets

proof.quote: The skeleton, in other words, runs a strict economy.
Tissue that is not loaded is treated as surplus and spent

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says the skeleton runs a strict economy and then explains what that means: tissue that is not loaded is treated as surplus and spent, with the osteocytes as the accountants. The sense is thrift, not a nation's markets.
distractorNotes: This is the common meaning, but the sentence is about a single skeleton managing its own tissue, not a nation.
Nothing in the sentence describes hardship; it describes a policy of not keeping what is unused.
The travel sense of economy class has no bearing on a sentence about bone.
The academic subject is a different sense; the skeleton is practicing thrift, not studying it.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following people would the author most likely expect to add the most bone to the legs over several months?
choices: A swimmer who covers two miles in the pool every morning
A person who stands for an hour each day holding a heavy pack without moving
A cyclist who rides long distances on flat roads several times a week
A person who walks briskly for an hour every evening on familiar streets
A person who performs a short daily set of hard, varied jumps

proof.quote: loading that is dynamic rather than static, forceful rather than prolonged, and unusual in its direction
a load applied and released a few dozen times a day was enough to maintain the bone and sometimes to add to it

questions.why: Paragraph 10's rule is that bone wants loading that is dynamic rather than static, forceful rather than prolonged, and unusual in direction, and that a few dozen loading cycles a day can be enough. A short set of hard, varied jumps fits every part of that rule.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 6 says swimming spares the skeleton and leaves swimmers with lighter bones.
Contradicted: the turkey experiments in paragraph 10 showed a steady, unchanging load did nothing to prevent bone loss.
Contradicted: paragraph 6 lists cyclists among athletes with lighter bones because their sport spares the skeleton.
Wrong fit: paragraph 10 says walking does less than assumed because it loads the skeleton in exactly the way it is used to.

questions.stem: According to the passage, astronauts who train hard on the station's resistance machine
choices: lose no bone at all, provided they train on it every day of the flight
show losses on standard density scans but none on finer measurements
have used it ever since the station's first long missions back in the late 1990s
lose far less bone by standard scans, though finer measures show some loss
no longer excrete extra calcium in their urine during the flight

proof.quote: lose markedly less bone by standard density scans, though finer measures of bone structure still record a loss

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says crews who train hard on the machine lose markedly less bone by standard density scans, though finer measures of bone structure still record a loss.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the passage says markedly less loss, not none, and finer measures still record a loss.
Reversed: it is the finer measures that still show loss while the standard scans look much better.
Wrong date: paragraph 10 says the machine has been aboard since late 2008.
Outside the passage: nothing says the machine removes the urinary calcium rise described in paragraph 8.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Wolff's law, despite flaws in its mathematics, remains the most accurate description of how bone grows
Bone is living tissue that its cells constantly rebuild in response to the loads it carries
Spaceflight is the single most damaging thing that can happen to the adult human skeleton
Resistance exercise can restore the bone that any person has lost at any age if it is forceful enough
Osteocytes are more important to the skeleton than osteoblasts and osteoclasts combined

proof.quote: taken apart and rebuilt without pause
bone is laid down where it is stressed and removed where it is not
a tissue in permanent negotiation with its own use

questions.why: Paragraph 1 introduces bone as tissue taken apart and rebuilt without pause, paragraph 5 states the rule that bone is laid down where stressed and removed where not, and paragraph 11 sums the skeleton up as a tissue in permanent negotiation with its own use. The spaceflight, bed rest, and exercise sections are all cases of that one idea.
distractorNotes: Too narrow and too strong: the author says the title of law flatters the claim, and Wolff is one historical thread.
Too extreme and never said: spaceflight is the sharpest demonstration, not the most damaging event.
Contradicted: paragraph 11 refuses to go as far as the enthusiasts who promise that any bone can be rebuilt at any age.
Too narrow: osteocytes set the terms, but the passage is about the whole remodeling system and what drives it.
